headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risks arise from shared file-based workflows; no direct shared channel is documented, so interaction risk is inferred.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A (botpress) is a customer-support bot with no documented isolation or provenance controls, while Agent B reads and writes files in a local development environment and processes file-backed notebooks. A shared filesystem or manual handoff could let attacker-controlled content in B be treated as instructions by A. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF Agent B writes untrusted content into a file that Agent A later ingests as chat or prompt text, injection is possible.
IF the two agents are connected through a shared workspace or copied transcripts, prompt injection risk increases.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Strip instructions from any file passed from B to A.
Require human review before A consumes B-generated text.
Disable automatic file ingestion into A where possible.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly touches configuration secrets and academic-paper data, and it has filesystem read/write plus allowlisted network egress. Agent A has no network egress and no data classes listed, but its support-bot role makes it a plausible consumer of B-produced text. Because a shared workspace or copied artifacts could expose B's secrets or paper data to A, the leakage pathway exists in default local-development setups, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF B stores secrets or paper data in files that A can read, leakage to A is possible.
IF A forwards B-originated content into logs or support responses, sensitive data can be exposed.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories.
Mount B's secret files read-only and exclude them from A.
Redact secrets before any handoff to A.
Review A outputs for accidental inclusion of B data.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and write files; Agent A can install packages. Even though B cannot modify git state and A has no write surface documented, both can mutate the local environment through package installation or file writes. The overlap is enough for conflicting changes in a shared workspace, but the absence of documented shared-state details keeps this below high.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory tree, file-level conflicts can occur.
IF A installs packages while B runs shell-based workflows, environment drift can break either agent.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Pin package versions for both agents.
Run one agent at a time during environment changes.
Snapshot the environment before package installs.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is a content-writing/RAG workflow that can produce answers from papers and metadata, and Agent A is a support bot that may present or act on text it receives. If B's output is treated as authoritative by A without verification, errors can cascade into user-facing responses. No direct verification step is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default orchestration.
conditions: IF B-generated summaries are forwarded to A without validation, A can repeat incorrect facts.
IF A uses B outputs as final answers, downstream errors become user-visible.
mitigations: Add a verification step before A uses B output.
Require citations for any factual claim passed from B to A.
Flag low-confidence B outputs for human review.
Limit A to paraphrasing only after validation.
requires-engineering: implement structured provenance checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B handles configuration secrets and academic-paper data in a local development environment, while Agent A is a support bot with no stated residency or retention controls. The pair therefore has a compliance gap around secret handling and retention, but there is no direct evidence of regulated PHI or a specific jurisdiction mismatch. Because the policies are undocumented, the safer medium severity is warranted.
conditions: IF B stores secrets in logs or notebooks that A can access, retention and disclosure controls may be violated.
IF the deployment handles regulated data classes not listed in the profiles, compliance risk increases.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of notebooks and logs.
Set short retention on shared artifacts.
Review access to any exported transcripts.
Document data residency for both agents.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion policies.
